overview.intro: The practical examination carries 30 of the subject’s 100 marks, and it assesses a different skill from the theory paper: turning a physical situation into measurements, and measurements into a result with a stated uncertainty. This chapter walks the whole prescribed course — the Section A and Section B experiments and activities exactly as the official document lists them — explains the working principle behind each, sets out what a complete record must contain, and finishes with the evaluation scheme so that the candidate knows precisely what is being marked. The theory of measurement from the Units and Measurements chapter is the common thread through every experiment here.

learn.title: The evaluation scheme and the record

blocks.text: The practical examination runs three hours for 30 marks and is graded on five components: two experiments, one from each section, at 7 marks each; the practical record covering experiments and activities, worth 5; one activity chosen from any section, worth 3; an investigatory project worth 3; and a viva on the experiments, activities and project worth 5. The record submitted at the annual examination must contain at least eight complete experiments — four from Section A and four from Section B — and at least six activities, three from each section, together with the project report. Understanding the arithmetic of the scheme changes how the time should be spent: the two experiments carry nearly half the marks and are performed under observation, so familiarity with the apparatus from the record work is worth more than any last-minute reading, while the viva rewards being able to state the principle of whatever is in front of you.

A complete record entry has a fixed anatomy, and examiners look for each part. Aim: the quantity being determined, stated with its symbol. Apparatus: every item with its range and least count. Theory: the formula with each symbol defined — this is where the Units and Measurements chapter earns its keep, since the dimensional consistency of the formula is checked at a glance. Diagram: a neat labelled circuit or arrangement, drawn from observation of the real setup rather than copied from a book. Observations: tabulated, with column headings carrying units and at least one sample calculation shown. Result: the value with units and, where the syllabus asks, the uncertainty. Precautions and sources of error: specific to the apparatus used, not generic sentences copied between experiments. That anatomy — aim, apparatus, theory, diagram, observations, result, precautions — is worth memorising as a checklist, because it also structures the viva answer when the examiner asks what an experiment is for.

learn.title: Section A: measurement, pendulum, friction, projectile

blocks.text: Section A opens with the measurement experiments that the whole course rests on. Vernier callipers measure external diameter, internal diameter and depth — the four jaws and the depth rod each have their role — with a least count of 0.01 cm, and the screw gauge measures wire diameter and sheet thickness at 0.01 mm, with zero error checked by closing the jaws and noted with its sign. The spherometer finds the radius of curvature of a spherical surface from the height of its central screw over three fixed legs, and the beam balance compares masses through the principle of moments. Each apparatus has its characteristic blunder: closing a screw gauge too tightly deforms the wire being measured, and reading a vernier without aligning the correct vernier division produces errors of a millimetre or more — both avoidable by the same habit of checking the zero and taking the reading slowly.

The pendulum experiments carry the marks for graphical work. Plotting period against length gives a curve, so the analysis plots T² against L — a straight line whose slope is 4π²/g, from which g follows. The standard refinement uses the effective length, measured to the centre of the bob, and either averaging ten oscillations for the period or, better, timing 20 and dividing — because a stopwatch’s reaction error of about 0.2 s is then a 1% error rather than 5%. The mass-variation experiment (same bob size, different masses) demonstrates that the period does not depend on mass, and the amplitude experiment notes the small-angle caveat: beyond roughly 10° the period lengthens, which is why the derivation’s approximation is quoted in the record’s precautions. Section A closes with friction — relating limiting friction to normal reaction by adding weights to a block and finding the coefficient as the slope of that graph — and the projectile experiment, which confirms the parabolic range-angle relation and locates the 45° maximum, both best analysed through the graph rather than individual readings.

items: Check zero error on every screw instrument and record its sign.
Pendulum: plot T² against L; slope = 4π²/g.
Time 20 oscillations, not one — the reaction error then divides away.
Effective length is measured to the centre of the bob.
Friction: coefficient = slope of limiting friction against normal reaction.
Projectile: the range-angle graph peaks at 45°.

learn.title: Section B: elasticity, fluids, heat and sound

blocks.text: Section B’s experiments connect directly to the theory chapters just studied. Young’s modulus comes from the extension of a loaded wire read by a micrometer — the graph of extension against load gives the slope needed for Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L), and the precautions are about avoiding kinking the wire and adding loads gently. The spring constant follows from load against extension (the slope IS k), and the gas-law experiment relates pressure and volume of a trapped air column at constant temperature, producing the p against 1/V straight line that verifies Boyle’s law. Surface tension is measured by capillary rise, h = 2γ/(ρgr) for a wetting liquid with a zero contact angle, and viscosity by timing a ball’s fall to its terminal velocity and applying Stokes’ law — each experiment’s formula lifted straight from its theory chapter, which is exactly the link the syllabus intends.

The heat and sound experiments complete the section. The cooling-curve experiment plots a hot body’s temperature against time and, through Newton’s law of cooling, compares two liquids or two surfaces; the specific heat of a solid by mixtures applies the calorimetry balance to find c, corrections for the calorimeter included; and the sonometer experiments verify the relations between a wire’s frequency, its length under constant tension (f ∝ 1/L) and its tension at constant frequency (f ∝ √T), which the standing-wave theory of the Waves chapter predicts. The resonance tube measures the speed of sound from the two resonance positions, the subtraction L₂ − L₁ = λ/2 removing the end correction — a refinement the viva loves to ask about. For all of these, the graph analysis carries the marks: straight-line plots with the variables chosen to linearise the relation, slopes computed, and the physical constant recovered from that slope with its units shown.

items: Young's modulus: extension-load graph; slope feeds Y = FL/(AΔL).
Spring constant: slope of the load-extension graph.
Boyle’s law: p against 1/V is a straight line through the origin.
Capillary rise gives surface tension; terminal velocity gives viscosity.
Sonometer: f ∝ 1/L at constant tension; f ∝ √T at constant frequency.
Resonance tube: λ/2 = L₂ − L₁ eliminates the end correction.

learn.title: Error analysis, graphs and the viva

blocks.text: Every experiment in this course ends in a graph, and the standard of graphical work is examinable in its own right. Choose axes so the expected relation appears as a straight line — plot T² against L, p against 1/V, extension against load — because a straight line’s slope is robust against scatter in a way that a curve’s position is not. Label both axes with the quantity and its unit, state the scale chosen, plot points as small crosses, draw the best-fit line by eye through the middle of the scatter (never join the dots), and compute the slope from two distant points on that line rather than adjacent plotted points. The slope then feeds the physical constant through the theory formula, with units carried through the whole computation — the single most common source of lost marks in otherwise correct practical answers is a dropped power of ten from an unconverted millimetre or centimetre.

Error analysis is the quantitative half of the same discipline. Absolute uncertainty comes from the instrument’s least count; relative uncertainties combine as the theory chapter taught, adding for products and quotients, and the final answer is quoted to the precision its uncertainty supports. A percentage-error statement for each experiment — which reading contributes most and why — is exactly the kind of viva answer that distinguishes a candidate who performed the experiment from one who copied a table. For the viva itself, the preparation is honest and simple: be able to state the aim, principle, formula and one precaution for every experiment in the record; explain any unfamiliar term on the apparatus (vernier constant, terminal velocity, end correction, least count); and answer the follow-up that connects the experiment to its theory chapter — why does the T²–L graph straighten the relation? what would happen to g if the bob were magnetised? The project, worth its three marks, should follow the same pattern: a question, a method, measured data, a graph and a conclusion, all in the candidate’s own words.

items: Linearise before plotting: T²–L, p–1/V, extension–load.
Axes labelled with quantity and unit; scale stated; best-fit line.
Slope from two far-apart points on the fitted line.
Carry units and powers of ten through every step.
Viva: know aim, principle, formula and one precaution for every record experiment.

questions.prompt: The least count of a standard vernier calliper is:
questions.explanation: One vernier division (0.9 mm) against one main-scale division (1 mm) gives a vernier constant of 0.1 mm = 0.01 cm.

questions.prompt: To find g from a simple pendulum, the graph that gives a straight line is:
questions.explanation: Since T = 2π√(L/g), T² = (4π²/g)L — a straight line through the origin whose slope is 4π²/g.

questions.prompt: In the resonance-tube experiment, using both resonance positions serves mainly to:
questions.explanation: Subtracting L₂ − L₁ = λ/2 removes the unknown end correction e, which a single reading cannot separate from λ/4.

questions.explanation: Two experiments at 7 marks each give 14 of the 30 — the largest single component of the scheme.

questions.explanation: A vernier calliper resolves 0.01 cm and a screw gauge 0.01 mm; every record must state the least count of each instrument it reads.

questions.explanation: Measuring to the suspension point instead systematically shortens L and skews g.

questions.prompt: List the sections a complete practical record entry must contain, and state the record requirements for the annual examination.
questions.answer: A complete record entry contains: (1) Aim — the quantity to be determined, with its symbol; (2) Apparatus — every item with range and least count; (3) Theory — the formula with each symbol defined and, ideally, its derivation outline; (4) Diagram — a neat labelled sketch of the actual arrangement; (5) Observations — recorded in a table whose headings carry units, with a sample calculation; (6) Result — the value with units and, where required, the uncertainty; and (7) Precautions and sources of error — specific to the apparatus actually used. The annual-examination record must include at least eight experiments, four from Section A and four from Section B, at least six activities — three from each section — and the report of the investigatory project carried out during the year. Each entry follows that same anatomy, which is also the structure the viva questions follow when the examiner picks an experiment at random from the file.
questions.explanation: All seven sections of the entry listed and the 8-experiment, 6-activity, project requirements stated.

questions.prompt: Describe the experiment to determine Young’s modulus of a steel wire by extension under load, including the graph plotted and the precautions taken.
questions.answer: Aim: to determine Young’s modulus Y of steel from the extension of a wire under load. Apparatus: a uniform steel wire fixed at the top with a hanger at the bottom, a metre scale, a micrometer to measure the diameter, and 0.5 kg weights. Theory: Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL), so plotting extension ΔL against load F gives a straight line whose slope is ΔL/F = L/(AY); hence Y = L/(A × slope). Observations: the diameter is measured at several points and orientations with the micrometer (least count 0.01 mm) to average out non-circularity; the unloaded length L is measured with the metre scale; then load is added in equal steps, the hanger reading recorded each time, and the same readings repeated while unloading to check for permanent set. Graph: ΔL against F — straight through the origin if Hooke’s law holds; the slope from two distant points on the best-fit line gives Y. Precautions: add weights gently to avoid shock loading; ensure the wire is straight and free of kinks; measure the diameter in two perpendicular directions; keep loads within the elastic limit so unloading retraces loading; and read the micrometer without over-tightening, which would compress the wire itself.
questions.explanation: Aim, apparatus, theory with the graph choice, observation practice including unloading, and at least four apparatus-specific precautions.

questions.prompt: Explain the simple-pendulum experiment for determining g, including the graph, the computation of g from its slope, and an error discussion.
questions.answer: Aim: to determine acceleration due to gravity g using a simple pendulum. Theory: T = 2π√(l/g), so T² = (4π²/g)l — a linear relation between T² and l whose slope m = 4π²/g, giving g = 4π²/m. Procedure: a pendulum bob is suspended by a fine thread; the effective length l (suspension point to the bob’s centre, found by adding the bob radius to the thread length) is measured with a metre scale; the time for 20 oscillations is taken with a stopwatch and divided by 20 to give T; this is repeated for several lengths spread over roughly 50 to 100 cm. Graph: T² against l, drawn as a best-fit straight line through the origin; the slope is computed from two far-apart points on the fitted line, and g = 4π²/slope. With a slope of about 4.03 s²/m, g = 4 × 9.87/4.03 ≈ 9.79 m/s², close to the standard 9.8. Error discussion: timing 20 oscillations divides the reaction error (about 0.2 s) to 0.01 s per period, roughly 0.1% — the single largest practical improvement available; measuring to the bob’s centre removes the systematic error of using the thread length alone; keeping the amplitude below about 10° honours the small-angle approximation on which the formula depends, since larger swings run slow and would depress the computed g; and the percentage-error statement should name the length measurement as the next largest contributor, since the metre scale resolves only to about 1 mm in 1000 mm, or 0.1%.
questions.explanation: Theory with the linearised relation, the procedure with the 20-swing timing, the slope computation, and a full error discussion naming at least two specific contributors.

questions.prompt: A candidate reports g = 9.1 m/s² from the pendulum experiment against the accepted 9.8 m/s². Diagnose the three most likely systematic causes, explain how each depresses the result, and state how the record would reveal each.
questions.answer: Diagnosis 1 — effective length measured to the suspension point rather than to the bob’s centre. The formula requires the distance to the centre of mass, and omitting the bob’s radius (say 1 cm on a 100 cm pendulum) underestimates l by about 1% in length, but since g is computed as 4π²l/T², an underestimated l returns a g low by the same proportion — here 9.8 × 0.99 ≈ 9.7, and several such centimetres across a shorter pendulum would deepen the deficit. The record reveals it if the tabulated l values are visibly the thread lengths, or if the T²–l line fails to pass near the origin, since a radius-length offset shifts every point equally. Diagnosis 2 — timing fewer oscillations than assumed, or miscounting them. Timing 10 swings but dividing by 20 doubles every measured period; because g ∝ 1/T², that depresses g by a factor of four — far more than the deficit here, but the milder version, counting 19 oscillations while dividing by 20, gives a 5% low period and roughly 10% low g. The observation table exposes this immediately if the recorded times for successive trials jump between plausible and doubled values. Diagnosis 3 — swinging the bob at a large amplitude. Beyond about 10° the true period exceeds the small-angle formula’s prediction, so the measured T is too large for the l used, and g = 4π²l/T² comes out low — a 15° swing gives roughly a 1% deficit, consistent in direction with the reported value. The record reveals it if the amplitude is not stated in the precautions (the honest record states “amplitude kept below 5°”), and the viva would confirm it by asking what approximation underlies the formula. General method: a systematic low result means either l measured short, T measured long, or the count mismatched — those three exhaust the formula’s levers, and each leaves its own fingerprint in the table or graph, which is why a complete record with stated amplitude, oscillation count and centre-of-mass length is the best defence against exactly this outcome.
questions.explanation: Three distinct systematic causes each tied to the g ∝ l/T² structure, the quantitative direction and rough size of each effect, and the specific record evidence that would expose it.
